pass_a_gloss: What is the reason for the silence of the many, and especially now, and for my being forced to be silent, both willingly and unwillingly, and to be compelled to silence. For I have neglected, in a way, the good and beautiful words, which are spoken or written by the chosen and approved men, with names and verbs, in a certain unimpeded sequence. And I, being less capable of this charming task, have not been able to accomplish it, which is truly a Greek work. But, on the other hand, this is now my eighth year, during which I have not been able to say or write anything, either great or small, nor have I heard anyone else speaking or writing, except for those wonderful men who have practiced the beautiful philosophy, to whom elegance and refinement of names are of little concern. They, placing their voices second, wish to examine and proclaim the matters themselves, with precision, not unwillingly, I think, but very willingly, the good and accurate things of the thoughts, though they may be unable to do so, having the sacred and divine word, and the word in the expressions, which is easy to speak, in the soul, which is difficult for a single human soul to contain, the two things, each one's own, and also human, and small. For if silence is somehow a friend and helper to the mind and discovery, the eloquent, on the other hand, is not found anywhere else, but in the voices and the continuous practice of them. But, on the other hand, the mind also seizes another kind of learning, and the mouth binds the tongue, if I wanted to say something, even small, to the Greek voice, our wonderful men, who now direct the affairs of all humans under the human rule, not being ignorant or unlearned, being themselves accurate and varied and wonderful, and being called the most Greek, having been expressed and handed down to the Roman voice, which is impressive and boastful and conforming to the royal authority, but burdensome to me. But, since the words are, in a way, images of the passions of our soul, to those who are able to speak, like good painters, and with technique, and with the material of colors, not only similar, but also varied and beautiful, to write the writings, without being hindered, we would agree.
pass_b_english: Why have so many fallen silent, again and again, and why am I, especially now, forced to hold my tongue, both willingly and unwillingly, compelled into silence? I have neglected, in a way, the good and beautiful words spoken or written by the chosen and approved men, in names and verbs, in an unbroken sequence. I am less naturally gifted for this charming task; I have not been able to accomplish what is truly a Greek work. Yet eight years have already passed for me since I have been able neither to speak nor to write anything at all, great or small, nor have I heard anyone else speaking or writing privately, or even delivering public panegyric and competitive speeches, except for those wonderful men who have pursued the beautiful philosophy. For them, elegance and refinement of names matter less; placing their voices second, they wish to examine and proclaim the matters themselves with precision, not unwillingly, I think, but very willingly, the good and accurate things of the thoughts, though they may be unable to do so, because they possess the sacred and God-given mind and the word in expressions that is easy to speak, two things that belong to each of two human souls, each one's own, and also human, and small, which a single human soul cannot contain. If silence is somehow a friend and helper to the mind and discovery, the eloquent word, on the other hand, is not found anywhere else but in voices and the continuous practice of them. But the mind also seizes another kind of learning with great force, and the mouth binds the tongue, if I wanted to say something, even a little, in the Greek voice. Our wonderful men, who now direct the affairs of all humans under human rule, are not ignorant nor unlearned; being themselves accurate, varied, and wonderful, and in a word the most Greek, they have been expressed and handed down to the Roman voice, which is impressive and boastful and conforms to the royal authority, yet burdensome to me. But since words are, in a way, images of the passions of our soul, to those who are able to speak, like good painters with the most technical skill and with the material of colors, not only similar but also varied and beautiful with the rich mixture of flowers to write the writings without being hindered, we would agree.
notes: The text is a panegyric to Origen, and the author is discussing the difficulty of speaking and writing about him.
